work.text: The composition and brushwork of Six Gentlemen are simpler compared to Ni Zan’s earlier paintings, such as Enjoying the Wilderness in an Autumn Grove (1339) and Water and Bamboo Dwelling (1343), which had been influenced by the styles of Dong Yuan and Zhao Mengfu.
From delicate and small-scale compositions in the 1350s and [earlier], Ni moved toward larger images that about 1360 settled into a pattern.

source.author: Richard M. Barnhart
source.title: Along the Border of Heaven: Sung and Yüan Paintings from the C. C. Wang Family Collection
source.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: Everyone of them is of his own class and quite different, but I admire them all and have no criticism to offer. I do not know anybody who would be their superior
moment.lead: Ni Zan on the older Yuan landscape masters, Zhao Mengfu and Huang Gongwang among them:

source.author: Ni Zan (Ni Tsan)
source.title: Ch’ing Pi Ko I Kao, translated in Osvald Sirén, A History of Early Chinese Painting, vol. II

moment.text: All these landscape painters were in later times classified as of the “Southern School”. They were said to continue the traditions of Tung Yuan, [Chü-jan], and Mi Fei, but the connection is more a matter of technical methods than of aesthetic ideals

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: A History of Early Chinese Painting, vol. II

matters.text: Ni Zan was born into an elite family who could afford the cost of a rigorous Confucian education for him in spite of the unavailability of high-paying governmental jobs that traditionally were the reward for such an education.
Born to wealth and good position, he cared nothing for the pleasures of social life and preferred to wander alone in the hills, conversing with priests and recluses.

source.author: John C. Ferguson
